newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Peter the Great fest to rekindle Dutch-Russian ties.
newsitem.headline: Peter the Great fest to rekindle Dutch-Russian ties.

text.p: Three centuries ago the father of modern-day Russia, Tsar Peter the Great, travelled to the Dutch Republic in search of the technology to bring his backward country up to date.

Working with saw in hand as a carpenter, Peter spent months learning the art of shipbuilding and other trades. He took back to Russia not only the knowhow to make his country a modern military power, but also a lifelong admiration for the Dutch way of doing things.
He even named his new capital in Dutch as "Sankt Peterburg".

Peter's visit in 1697-8 proved to be the start of a mutually beneficial alliance, giving Russia its first navy and generating substantial revenues for Dutch coffers until all ties were abruptly severed in the bloody Russian revolution of 1917.
Now the Dutch are seeking to rekindle the warmth of those old relations with an eye to the commercial opportunities offered by Russia's emerging free-market economy.

The Peter the Great Manifestation, a year-long programme of cultural and business events, kicks off simultaneously in St Petersburg and Zaandam near Amsterdam on Saturday with activities planned in more than a dozen cities including Moscow, The Hague and Rotterdam.

"The driving force behind the manifestation is to strengthen existing relations and to forge new ties," said Peter Buwalda, head of the festival's steering committee and a former Dutch ambassador to Moscow.
"It all started very spontaneously with lots of Dutch museums and universities planning individual initiatives and just snowballed from there," he said in an interview.
"When we learned that Russia was planning a commemoration to mark the founding of its navy we decided to pool resources."
The Dutch festivities will begin with a re-enactment of the Tsar's landing in Zaandam, the town north of Amsterdam where the Russian emperor plied his trade as ship's carpenter.
A two-day cultural programme featuring a parade of historic Dutch and Russian ships, folk-dancing and a mock sea-battle will be opened by Dutch Princess Margriet, sister of Queen Beatrix.
Subsequent events being staged throughout the Netherlands include exhibitions, ballet and theatrical performances.
The centre of gravity, however, clearly lies in Russia, where the Netherlands has seized on the anniversary as a calling card for Dutch companies.
Dutch heir to the throne Crown Prince Willem-Alexander travels to St Petersburg on Saturday to launch a month-long "Window on the Netherlands" showcasing Dutch arts and business.
He will be joined on his four-day visit by a heavyweight government delegation including Prime Minister Wim Kok and his ministers for foreign trade, agriculture and transport.

Alongside cultural events ranging from classical concerts to vaudeville performances, the programme features a series of seminars aimed at bringing Dutch and Russian companies together, a trade fair and an exhibition promoting the Netherlands as a distribution hub.
"Thanks in part to history, present-day Russians see the Netherlands as an attractive, technologically advanced trading partner," Buwalda said. "Obviously we are eager to build on that."
The Netherlands currently ranks as Russia's ninth-largest trading partner, accounting for 3.1 percent of Russia's total trade in the first three months of this year.
Dutch exports to the Russian federation amounted to 2.74 billion guilders last year.
